studyPages.title: What Is Fire
studyPages.body:
WHAT IS FIRE
====

WHAT YOU WILL LEARN
----
• Explain what is fire in your own words.
• Give a real Kenyan example that shows what is fire.
• Avoid a common mistake learners make about what is fire.

INTRODUCTION
----
Around a hardware shop in Nakuru, learners meet science ideas without opening a textbook. Fires can be classified between four and seven classes. This page explains what is fire so you can recognise it, name it correctly, and use it safely.

MAIN NOTES
----
• Fires can be classified between four and seven classes.
• The following are six classes of fire mostly widely used and accepted.
• Fires that burn materials such as wood, cloth, paper and plastics.
• Fires that involve liquids such as grease, oils, paraffin, petrol, diesel and alcohol.
• Fires that involve gases such as propane, butane and methane.
• Fires that are ignited by combustible metals such as potassium, sodium, aluminium and magnesium.
• These fires are ignited by cooking oil and animal fats.

WORKED EXAMPLE
----
At a hardware shop in Nakuru, a Grade 8 learner tests the idea of what is fire. Observation: Fires can be classified between four and seven classes. The learner then explains the science in their own words, checks a symbol or formula if one applies (for example H₂O, NaCl, Fe, or P = F / A), and writes a short conclusion that matches the definition on this page.

IN EVERYDAY LIFE
----
In everyday life around a hardware shop in Nakuru, you can spot what is fire when you look carefully at materials, heat, food, tools, or living things. Safety tip: follow teacher and lab rules, protect your eyes when heating, never taste unknown chemicals, and raise the alarm early if you see smoke or fire.

SUMMARY
----
• Fires can be classified between four and seven classes.
• The following are six classes of fire mostly widely used and accepted.
• Fires that burn materials such as wood, cloth, paper and plastics.
• Fires that involve liquids such as grease, oils, paraffin, petrol, diesel and alcohol.

REVISION QUESTIONS
----
1. Define what is fire in your own words and give one clear example.
2. Describe a situation at a hardware shop in Nakuru that shows what is fire, and explain the science involved.
3. A learner makes a mistake about what is fire. State a likely wrong idea, correct it, and justify your correction with facts from this page.

ANSWERS
----
1. Fires can be classified between four and seven classes. Example: you can connect this idea to something real at home, school, market, or shamba — for instance materials, heat, food, tools, or living cells related to what is fire.
2. At a hardware shop in Nakuru, the situation shows what is fire because the materials or process match the definition on this page. First name what you observe. Next link it to the correct scientific idea (including any correct symbol or formula such as H₂O, NaCl, Fe, or P = F / A). Finally say why the correct idea helps you stay accurate or safe.
3. A common wrong idea is to treat what is fire as if it were a different, neighbouring concept, or to ignore a key rule (for example symbol capitalization, physical versus chemical change, or force and area in pressure). The correction is: Combustion basics for Grade 8. Use the worked example on this page as evidence that the corrected statement fits the facts.

studyPages.title: The Fire Triangle
studyPages.body:
THE FIRE TRIANGLE
====

WHAT YOU WILL LEARN
----
• Explain the fire triangle in your own words.
• Give a real Kenyan example that shows the fire triangle.
• Avoid a common mistake learners make about the fire triangle.

INTRODUCTION
----
Around a kitchen in Kisumu, learners meet science ideas without opening a textbook. A fire triangle in a simple model of understanding the components of fire which are fuel, heat and oxygen. This page explains the fire triangle so you can recognise it, name it correctly, and use it safely.

MAIN NOTES
----
• A fire needs three things at the same time: fuel, heat, and oxygen. Together they form the fire triangle.
• Fuel is anything that can burn, such as wood, paper, petrol, or cooking oil.
• Heat raises the fuel to its ignition temperature.
• Oxygen from the air supports burning. If you remove any one side of the triangle, the fire can go out.

WORKED EXAMPLE
----
At a market stall, cooking oil on a cloth catches fire. Owino reaches for a bucket of water. Sergeant Achieng stops him: for an oil fire, water can spread the burning fuel. Instead they cut the heat/oxygen carefully with a cover and move people away. Removing one side of the fire triangle matters more than panic.

IN EVERYDAY LIFE
----
In everyday life around a kitchen in Kisumu, you can spot the fire triangle when you look carefully at materials, heat, food, tools, or living things. Safety tip: follow teacher and lab rules, protect your eyes when heating, never taste unknown chemicals, and raise the alarm early if you see smoke or fire.

SUMMARY
----
• A fire needs three things at the same time: fuel, heat, and oxygen. Together they form the fire triangle.
• Fuel is anything that can burn, such as wood, paper, petrol, or cooking oil.
• Heat raises the fuel to its ignition temperature.
• Oxygen from the air supports burning. If you remove any one side of the triangle, the fire can go out.

REMOVING FUEL FROM A FIRE
====

WHAT YOU WILL LEARN
----
• Explain removing fuel from a fire in your own words.
• Give a real Kenyan example that shows removing fuel from a fire.
• Avoid a common mistake learners make about removing fuel from a fire.

INTRODUCTION
----
Around Lake Magadi salt works, learners meet science ideas without opening a textbook. Helps us to remove sources of ignition (sparks, smoking, flames or hot surfaces) when working with flammable and combustible products. This page explains removing fuel from a fire so you can recognise it, name it correctly, and use it safely.

MAIN NOTES
----
• Helps us to remove sources of ignition (sparks, smoking, flames or hot surfaces) when working with flammable and combustible products.
• This will help to prevent the fire from starting and spreading.
• A water fire extinguisher would be the safest way of doing this.
• However, these extinguishers cannot be used on all types of fire.\.
• This can be achieved by using either a carbon (IV) oxide or a form fire extinguisher.
• Fire extinguisher come in different types depending on the kind of environment you are in. Some places such as school, work or home, one or more types of fire extinguishers may be required.
